title: Why Do We Forget Names?
paragraphs: Most people have had this experience: you meet someone at a party, they tell you their name, and ten seconds later it has completely disappeared from your mind. You remember their face, their job and even the colour of their shirt, but the name is gone.

Psychologists have a simple explanation. When we are introduced to someone, our attention is divided. We are thinking about what to say next, how we look and whether we are making a good impression. The name arrives at exactly the moment when our mind is busy with other things, so it never really enters our memory.

Names are also difficult because they carry very little meaning. If someone tells you they are a baker, your brain connects the word to smells, bread and early mornings. A name like 'Daniel' or 'Selin', on the other hand, gives the brain nothing to hold on to.

There are a few tricks that can help. Repeat the name as soon as you hear it: "Nice to meet you, Daniel." Use it once more during the conversation. Some people also create a small picture in their mind, for example imagining Daniel standing in a lion's den. It sounds silly, but connecting a name to an image makes it much easier to remember.
So if you forget someone's name, do not worry too much. It does not mean you are not interested in them. It simply means your brain was doing too many things at once.

title: Who Owns a Photograph?
paragraphs: Every day, millions of photographs are shared online. Many people assume that once a picture is on the internet, anyone can use it. In most countries, however, this is not true. The law usually gives the person who took the photograph, not the person in it, the right to decide how it is copied and shared. This right is called copyright.

Copyright exists automatically. A photographer does not need to register the picture or add a special symbol; the protection begins at the moment the photo is taken. If a company uses the image in an advertisement without permission, the photographer can ask for it to be removed and, in some cases, demand payment.

The situation becomes more complicated when a photograph shows a recognisable person. Many legal systems also protect people's image and privacy. A photographer may own the copyright, but that does not always mean they can use a stranger's face to sell a product without the stranger's consent.

There are exceptions. Short extracts may often be used for news reporting, criticism or education, although the rules differ from country to country. Some photographers also choose to share their work under open licences that allow others to reuse it freely, as long as they give credit.

The simple lesson is this: a picture being easy to download does not mean it is free to use. Before you publish someone else's photograph, it is worth checking who owns it and what permission you need.

title: The Invisible Rules of the Queue
paragraphs: Waiting in line seems like one of the simplest things people do. Yet sociologists find queues fascinating, because they are full of rules that nobody writes down but almost everybody follows.

The most important rule is fairness: whoever arrives first should be served first. When someone pushes to the front, other people often feel angry, even if they lose only a few seconds. What upsets them is not the time but the feeling that the rule has been broken.

Queues also have rules about space. People usually leave a small gap between themselves and the person in front. If you stand too close, others feel uncomfortable; if you leave too much space, someone may think you are not in the line at all.

These rules are not the same everywhere. In some countries, people form neat single lines at bus stops. In others, a crowd gathers and everyone knows, without speaking, who came first. Newcomers to a country often find these differences confusing.
Studying queues shows something important about society. Order does not always depend on police, signs or laws. Very often, it depends on shared expectations that people learn by watching each other.

title: Gifts That Build Relationships
paragraphs: In many cultures, giving a gift is never just about the object itself. Anthropologists have long argued that gifts create relationships and obligations between people. When you receive something, you are expected, sooner or later, to give something back.

One well-known example comes from islands in the western Pacific, where people once travelled long distances by canoe to exchange necklaces and armbands. The objects had little practical use, and they were not kept for ever; instead, they moved from person to person in a great circle. What mattered was the network of partnerships the exchange created.

Similar ideas can be found much closer to home. Many families in Turkey return a neighbour's plate filled with food rather than empty. Returning it empty would feel strange, almost rude, because the exchange is meant to continue.

Gifts can also express status. A very expensive present may put the receiver in an uncomfortable position if they cannot return something of similar value. In this sense, a gift can be generous and demanding at the same time.

Anthropologists therefore suggest looking at gifts as a kind of language. Through what we give, when we give it and how we respond, we communicate respect, friendship and our place within a community.

title: Learning from Mistakes in the Classroom
paragraphs: Many students are afraid of making mistakes. They stay silent in class because they do not want to give a wrong answer in front of others. Teachers and researchers, however, increasingly see mistakes as an essential part of learning.

When we get something wrong and then find the correct answer, our brains work harder than when we simply read the answer. This extra effort helps us remember the information for longer. In other words, a mistake that is corrected can be more useful than a correct guess.

For this reason, some teachers ask students to try a problem before explaining how to solve it. Students often fail at first, but the lesson that follows makes more sense because they already understand what the difficulty is.

The atmosphere of the classroom matters too. If students feel that mistakes will be laughed at, they will avoid taking risks. Teachers who respond calmly, and even show their own mistakes, help students feel safe enough to try.
Of course, not every mistake is helpful. Repeating the same error without noticing it teaches very little. The key is to notice the mistake, understand why it happened and try again.
